newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German Kinkel says France no EMU threat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German Kinkel says France no EMU threat.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel insisted on Tuesday that France's call for time to study a key element of Europe's proposed currency union would not hold back plans for the project.
"France's behaviour will in no way mean we are going to be hamstrung," Kinkel told reporters at a reception in Bonn. "I can't see that there is a change in the basic position of the French."

Kinkel was speaking after Dominique Strauss-Kahn, Finance Minister of France's newly-installed Socialist government, told EU counterparts in Luxembourg on Monday that Paris wanted to study the stability pact within Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

The pact, a German initiative concluded after tough negotiations in Dublin last December, is intended to ensure the stability of the euro by censuring EMU participants which do not live up to agreed measurements of economic performance.
It was supposed to be ratified by EU leaders when they meet in Amsterdam next week.

But Strauss-Kahn said that while France did not want to renegotiate the pact, it would be unable to endorse the agreement until after a National Assembly debate planned for June 19, two days after the Amsterdam summit.
German government sources said there was no strict link between the Amsterdam summit and the stability pact.

Kinkel said he understood perfectly well that the new French government, which has been in office just over a week, needed more time to reflect on the pact and that this period of reflection did not necessarily endanger the project.
"(Plans for) the stability pact remain, the euro will arrive and the stability pact will arrive," Kinkel said.

German media on Tuesday styled the French move as an attempt to delay in the pact and accused France, whose new government has said it opposes further austerity measures to qualify for EMU, of seeking to thwart the project.
